mcqs.question: Why must a quorum threshold be a strict majority, floor(N/2)+1, rather than some smaller fraction of N?
options: A smaller fraction is always faster to compute at runtime
A strict majority is required by most cloud providers' SLAs
It makes leader election unnecessary entirely
A strict majority guarantees no two disjoint groups of nodes can both reach the threshold at the same time, which is what prevents two conflicting quorums from both succeeding
mcqs.explanation: The strict-majority requirement is what mathematically guarantees any two quorum-sized groups must overlap, ruling out two disjoint groups both succeeding at once. It isn't about computation speed, isn't an SLA requirement, and quorum doesn't eliminate the need for leader election — it's often used within it.

mcqs.question: Why does requiring read quorum (R) plus write quorum (W) to exceed total nodes (N) guarantee a read sees the latest write?
options: It forces every single node to be reachable before any operation is allowed
It guarantees any read quorum and any write quorum must share at least one common node, and that node has the latest write
It doubles the write throughput of the system
It removes the need for replication entirely
mcqs.explanation: R + W > N is exactly the condition that forces overlap between any read group and any write group, guaranteeing the read touches at least one node that has the latest committed write. It doesn't require full-cluster reachability, doesn't affect throughput directly, and doesn't remove the need for replication — it's a property of how replicas are queried.

mcqs.question: Why is an even number of nodes a weaker choice for a quorum-based cluster than an odd number?
options: Even-sized clusters cannot perform leader election at all
An even-sized cluster can split into two exactly equal halves, neither reaching a strict majority, losing availability in a scenario an odd-sized cluster structurally can't hit
Even numbers of nodes always cost more to run in the cloud
Even-sized clusters require a different quorum formula entirely
mcqs.explanation: The specific risk is an exact even split leaving neither half with a majority — safe, but a loss of availability an odd-sized cluster avoids since it can't split into two equal halves. Leader election still works on even clusters, cost isn't inherently different, and the formula (floor(N/2)+1) is the same regardless of parity.

mcqs.question: Why is using exactly half the nodes as the quorum threshold incorrect?
options: Two disjoint groups can each independently contain exactly half the nodes and both hit the threshold at the same time, which is the split-brain scenario quorum is meant to prevent
Exactly half is actually the correct and standard quorum threshold
Half-sized quorums are only a problem in clusters larger than 100 nodes
Half-sized quorums make writes permanently unavailable
mcqs.explanation: Exactly half fails to guarantee overlap — two separate, non-overlapping groups can each reach exactly half the nodes simultaneously, defeating the purpose of quorum. The correct threshold is strictly more than half; this issue applies at any cluster size, and it doesn't make writes permanently unavailable, just unsafe against split-brain.
